section.title: Perfected Through Suffering
section.sectionRationale: Having exalted the Son above the angels, the writer now explains why He was made lower than the angels for a while. Quoting Psalm 8, he shows that the destiny of humanity, dominion over the world to come, is secured in Jesus, who tasted death for everyone, and who became a merciful high priest by sharing our flesh and our suffering.
section.thesis: Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while, fulfills humanity's calling to glory by tasting death for everyone; sharing fully in our flesh and blood, He destroys the devil, frees those enslaved by fear of death, and becomes a merciful and faithful high priest who makes atonement and helps the tempted.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the world to come subjected not to angels but to man in Psalm 8; the sight of Jesus crowned through suffering; the Son unashamed to call us brothers; and the incarnation by which He conquers death and becomes our merciful high priest.

verses.text: For it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come, about which we are speaking.
But somewhere it is testified in these words: “What is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?
You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor
and placed everything under his feet.” When God subjected all things to him, He left nothing outside of his control. Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him.

units.label: We see Jesus, crowned through suffering
units.note: the author of salvation made perfect

verses.text: But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone.
In bringing many sons to glory, it was fitting for God, for whom and through whom all things exist, to make the {{archegos|author}} of their salvation {{teleioo|perfect}} through suffering.

units.label: Not ashamed to call them brothers

verses.text: For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them {{adelphos|brothers}}.
He says: “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly.”
And again: “I will put My trust in Him.” And once again: “Here am I, and the children God has given Me.”

units.label: Flesh and blood, the merciful high priest

verses.text: Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,
and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.
For surely it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham.

For this reason He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, in order to make {{hilaskomai|atonement}} for the sins of the people.
Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted.

archegos.gloss: A pioneer, founder, leader, or author, one who blazes a trail others follow. Jesus is the archēgos of salvation, the trailblazer who goes ahead through suffering and death into glory, opening the way and leading many sons after Him.

teleioo.gloss: To make perfect, complete, or fully qualified, to bring to the intended goal. The Son was not morally improved; He was made complete for His saving office, fully fitted through real suffering to be the sympathetic and effective high priest.

adelphos.gloss: A brother. The Son who sanctifies and those He sanctifies share one family, so He is not ashamed to call them brothers. His true humanity binds Him to His people in a bond He openly owns.

hilaskomai.gloss: To make atonement, to propitiate, to turn away wrath by a sufficient offering. As high priest Jesus makes atonement for the sins of the people, satisfying God's just judgment and reconciling sinners to God through His own death.

basic.context: If the Son is so much greater than angels, why did He become lower than them, a suffering human? This passage answers. God made humanity to rule the world, but we do not yet see that rule realized because of sin. We do, however, see Jesus, who became human, tasted death for everyone, and was crowned with glory. By sharing our flesh He defeats death and becomes our merciful high priest.
basic.hermeneutics: The writer reads Psalm 8, about humanity's dignity, as fulfilled in Jesus, the true man. Watch the move from 'we do not see everything subject to him' to 'but we see Jesus'. The unrealized destiny of humanity is secured in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is the archēgos, the pioneer, of salvation, made teleios, complete, through suffering. He calls His people adelphoi, brothers. As high priest He came to hilaskesthai, to make atonement, for their sins.
basic.typology: Adam was crowned to rule and lost it; Jesus, the last Adam, regains the crown through suffering. The high priest who made atonement on the Day of Atonement foreshadows Jesus, the merciful and faithful high priest who makes atonement once for all.
basic.christ: Christ is the true human who fulfills Psalm 8, the trailblazer who leads many sons to glory, the brother unashamed of His people, the conqueror of the devil and death, and the merciful high priest who makes atonement and helps the tempted because He was tempted Himself.
basic.god: It was fitting for God, for whom and through whom all things exist, to save this way, through the suffering of His Son. God brings many sons to glory, and does so by grace, that Jesus might taste death for everyone.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 8 celebrates man crowned with glory. 1 Corinthians 15 calls Christ the last Adam. Philippians 2 traces His humbling and exaltation. Hebrews 4 returns to the sympathetic high priest.
basic.oneStory: Humanity was made to reign and fell; the story runs to Jesus, the true man who reclaims the crown through the cross, defeats death, and gathers many brothers into glory.

context.literary:
This section is the hinge between two movements of the letter. Chapter 1 proved the Son's rank with seven Old Testament quotations; the warning of Hebrews 2:1-4 told the readers what happens if they drift from so great a salvation; and now verse 5 opens with a small word, 'for', that explains why a Son who outranks the angels would ever be seen beneath them. The argument runs on three tracks. First comes a Scripture, Psalm 8 in verses 6 to 8a, introduced with the studied vagueness 'somewhere it is testified', as though who held the pen matters less than who speaks through it. Second comes the writer's own pivot in verses 8b and 9, the pair of verbs 'we do not see' and 'we see', which sets present experience against present faith. Third comes the long explanation in verses 10 to 18, where two further quotations, Psalm 22:22 and Isaiah 8:17-18, are placed on the lips of Jesus Himself.

Suffering is the thread that ties the whole piece together. The crowning of verse 9 comes 'because He suffered death', verse 10 speaks of perfection 'through suffering', and verse 18 closes the unit with 'He Himself suffered when He was tempted'. That is an inclusion: the passage begins and ends on the cost Jesus paid. Notice too the family vocabulary that grows through the section, sons in verse 10, brothers in verses 11 and 12, children in verses 13 and 14, descendants of Abraham in verse 16, brothers again in verse 17.

Finally, verse 17 is a table of contents for the next stretch of the letter. 'Merciful' is taken up in 4:14 to 5:10, where the high priest deals gently with the ignorant, and 'faithful' is taken up in 3:1-6, where Jesus is set beside Moses. Hebrews is what the writer calls a 'word of exhortation', Hebrews 13:22, and it alternates doctrine and appeal. Here the doctrine is the incarnation, and the appeal waits in the last line: because He was tempted, He can help.
context.historical:
The first readers were Jewish believers under pressure, tempted to slip back into the safety of the older worship. For them angels were not a footnote. Jewish tradition made angels the go-betweens at Sinai, an idea that echoes in Hebrews 2:2, Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19, and a long line of Jewish thought saw angels as the guardians of the nations. A Messiah who was 'lower than the angels' therefore sounded like a demotion, and a crucified Messiah was worse. The law spoke of the one hung on a tree as under a curse, Deuteronomy 21:23, and the cross was the most shameful death the Roman world knew. Hebrews faces this head on, speaking later of Jesus 'scorning its shame', Hebrews 12:2, and of the 'disgrace He bore', Hebrews 13:13.

The passage also meets a fear that every ancient hearer carried. Death was the great unconquered enemy, and the writer speaks of people held 'in slavery by their fear of death' for 'all their lives', verse 15. That is the language of Israel's own story, where the people were once in bondage in Egypt until a lamb's blood marked their doors, Exodus 12:12-13, and where death moved through every house that was unmarked. The readers knew the rhythm of Passover and could feel the force of 'free'.

Then there is the priesthood. Israel's high priest was chosen 'from among men', Hebrews 5:1, and once a year entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement, Leviticus 16:15-16. The writer's claim that Jesus had to be 'made like His brothers in every way' answers a question the readers would have asked at once: how can one who is the Son of God serve as a priest taken from human beings? The letter does not name its author or date, but its argument is aimed at people who knew the Greek Old Testament well, since it quotes the Greek wording of Psalm 8.
context.canonical:
Psalm 8 gathers up Genesis 1:26-28, where humanity is made in God's image and given charge over fish, birds and beasts. When Psalm 8 is read later in Scripture it is always read as something still unfinished. Paul quotes the same line, 'He has put everything under His feet', in 1 Corinthians 15:27 and Ephesians 1:22 and gives it to the risen Christ, with the church sharing His fullness. In Matthew 21:16 Jesus uses an earlier line of the same psalm, from verse 2, to answer indignant priests. Hebrews takes the psalm the next step: the human destiny that Adam forfeited is held for us in the one true man.

The other two quotations are chosen with equal care. Psalm 22 is the psalm that begins with the cry of abandonment that Jesus took up on the cross, Matthew 27:46, and its verse 22 is the turn from anguish to praise in the congregation, followed by the promise that God 'has not hidden His face from him', Psalm 22:24. Isaiah 8:17-18 belongs to a passage of waiting in a dark hour, with children given to the prophet as signs, and Hebrews hears in it the voice of the Son trusting the Father and presenting the family given to Him.

The themes of verses 14 to 18 run through the New Testament. The destruction of the devil's work is stated in 1 John 3:8, the conquest of death in 1 Corinthians 15:26 and Revelation 1:18, and the Son's entry into our nature in Romans 8:3, Galatians 4:4-5 and Philippians 2:6-8. His priestly work is spelled out in Hebrews 4:14-16, 7:26-28 and 9:11-14, and the same Greek word for 'pioneer' reappears in Acts 3:15, 5:31 and Hebrews 12:2. Together these texts show that the thoughts of this passage are not a side road in the New Testament but its main highway.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer is a pastor, and his aim is to rescue weary Christians from a conclusion that seems reasonable: if Jesus is so glorious, His suffering must have been a mistake, and a faith that leads to suffering must be a mistake too. He wants the readers to see that the road of suffering is the very road God chose, and that God chose it because it was fitting, a word that answers the thought of an arbitrary or helpless God. Glory and suffering are not enemies in this plan; suffering is the path by which the Son leads many others to glory.

He wants them to see two things about their own place in this story. First, they are not left among the unseen: the words 'but we see Jesus' are placed against the admission that 'we do not see everything subject to him' on purpose, so that faith is given something to look at while the world still looks unfinished. Second, they are family. The Son is not ashamed to call them brothers, so their weakness does not put them outside His care. And he wants them to act on the last line: since He was tempted, those who are tempted may run to Him for help rather than hide from Him in shame.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this passage is exposition. It describes what the Son did and why, and it quotes the Psalms and Isaiah to ground that description. It is not a command to suffer, nor does it say that every hardship carries the same meaning as the Son's. Verse 10 speaks of the unique suffering of the pioneer, and verse 17 speaks of atonement that no believer can add to. Applying the passage means resting in what He has done, not repeating it.

The prescriptions are mostly implied and gentle. The reader is to 'see Jesus' rather than demand to see everything subject to us, to trust the Son who calls us brothers, to stop living under the fear of death, and to bring temptation to Him as the one 'able to help'. Care is needed with verse 18: it does not say that temptation is harmless or that Jesus excuses sin. It says that someone who knows temptation from the inside stands ready to help in the middle of it, which is a reason to come to Him early and often.

debates.question: What does it mean that Jesus was 'made perfect' through suffering?

views.label: Fully qualified for His saving office
views.case: The verb is teleioo, to bring to an intended end. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the consecration of priests, so that 'to perfect' can mean to install someone in office, Leviticus 8:33. Hebrews 5:8-9 says He 'learned obedience from what He suffered' and, 'having been made perfect', became the source of salvation. On this reading Jesus gained no moral improvement; He was brought through the experiences that made Him a fully fitted pioneer and priest.

views.label: Moral growth under trial
views.case: Some read the verb as a growth in obedience and character as His sufferings tested Him. The difficulty is that the letter insists He was 'without sin', Hebrews 4:15, and 'unblemished', Hebrews 9:14, so any growth has to be in experience and in the proving of a holiness already complete.

debates.bearing: The two readings meet at the point that matters. His perfecting did not remove a flaw; it completed His qualification to help sinners by passing through real human suffering, and it gives the believer's own trials a purpose.

debates.question: Is the death of Jesus in verse 17 a propitiation of God or an expiation of sin?

views.label: Propitiation, turning aside God's just wrath
views.case: The BSB footnote gives 'or to make propitiation'. Many read hilaskomai in light of Romans 3:25 and 1 John 4:10, where the sacrifice meets the demand of God's holiness. Verse 17 describes service 'to God' as high priest, and the sins of the people are the matter before Him.

views.label: Expiation, cleansing and covering sin
views.case: Others point out that in Greek the object of the verb here is 'the sins', not God, and that the Old Testament sin offering is chiefly about purging defilement, Leviticus 16:16. On this view the emphasis falls on removing the stain and breaking sin's power.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Leviticus 16 joins cleansing and satisfaction in one rite: the blood purges the sanctuary and also stands between a holy God and a sinful people. Hebrews 9:13-14 speaks of purifying the conscience by the blood of Christ.

debates.bearing: Whichever word is preferred, the text insists that sin is dealt with at its root and that the cost was borne by the priest Himself, so that the sinner's access to God is open and not merely tolerated.

debates.question: For whom did Jesus 'taste death' in verse 9?

views.label: Every one of the sons being brought to glory
views.case: The Greek reads 'for every one', and the next verse speaks of 'many sons'. On this view the scope of the sentence is set by what follows: those He leads to glory, those He sanctifies, His brothers and the descendants of Abraham in verse 16.

views.label: Everyone without exception
views.case: Others take the phrase at face value as a universal offer, matching 1 John 2:2, 'not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world', and say that the cross is sufficient for all.

debates.bearing: Both agree that the death was real, substitutionary and sufficient, and that it is Jesus who tastes it, the strongest word in the passage for the cost to Him.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with a small phrase that carries a large choice. The Greek of Psalm 8:5, which Hebrews quotes, says humanity was made 'brachy ti' lower than the angels, and the BSB footnote notes 'or a little while lower'. The phrase can mean a little in degree or a little in time. Hebrews hears the second meaning in verse 9, 'a little while lower', since Jesus' humiliation was a short season ending in crowning. The Hebrew of the psalm has Elohim where the Greek has angels, a difference the footnote also records, and the writer simply follows the Greek.

The verb 'taste' in verse 9 is geuomai, to experience from the inside, and it is a mark of how real the death was. It is Jesus who tastes death 'for everyone', the preposition huper meaning on behalf of. Some early witnesses read 'apart from God' where most read 'by the grace of God', and the great majority of manuscripts keep grace, which fits the whole tone of the passage.

In verse 10 the key word is eprepen, 'it was fitting'. The writer does not say it was necessary in the sense of something forced on God from outside; he says it fit who God is, 'for whom and through whom all things exist'. The cross is not a detour around God's character but a display of it.

Verse 11 puts two present participles side by side: ho hagiazon, 'the One who sanctifies', and hoi hagiazomenoi, 'those who are sanctified'. The phrase 'of the same family' is Greek ex henos, 'of one', and the thing it means is deliberately open: one Father, one nature, one origin. Hebrews later uses a related verb for the single offering by which believers 'have been sanctified', Hebrews 10:10.

In verse 14 two different verbs describe the sharing. The children 'have' flesh and blood in a shared and continuing way, but He 'too shared' in it, paraplesios, 'in just the same way', in a decisive act. The aim is stated with katargeo, to render powerless or put out of action, the same verb Paul uses of death in 1 Corinthians 15:26. The devil is not annihilated at the cross but stripped of his weapon.

In verse 16 the verb translated 'helps' is epilambanomai, literally 'to take hold of'. Hebrews 8:9 uses the same verb when it says God 'took them by the hand' to lead them out of Egypt. The image is of a rescuer reaching down to grip someone who cannot rise.

Finally, in verse 18 the word for help is boetheo, to run toward a cry, and it is joined with dynatai, 'He is able'. The sentence puts together power and sympathy: He can help, because He has stood where the tempted stand. The verb for being tempted is peirazo, which can also mean to be tested, and the passage allows both shades.

typology.type: Adam, the king of creation in Psalm 8
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 1:26-28 gives humanity rule over the creatures, and Psalm 8 sings that dignity. Adam lost it, so that 'we do not see everything subject to him', verse 8. Paul calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come', Romans 5:14, and Jesus is the man in whom Psalm 8 is true. He is crowned with glory and honour and all things are being placed under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:27. The type falls short because Adam's rule could be lost by one act, while the dominion of Christ comes with the defeat of death itself.

Israel was held in slavery under a king whose power was real and whose house was struck by death, Exodus 12:29-30. Hebrews hears an echo in verse 15, where the slaves are those 'held in slavery by their fear of death' and the one who holds the power of death is the devil. Jesus is the deliverer who does not merely lead people out; He breaks the master's power by dying. The text does not name Exodus here, so the link rests on the shared language of freedom from bondage, but later Scripture draws it, as in 1 Corinthians 5:7, where Christ is our Passover lamb.

typology.type: The high priest taken from among his brothers
typology.fulfillment: Israel's high priest bore the people's sins and entered once a year to make atonement, Leviticus 16:15-16, and he was one of them, a man 'beset by weakness', Hebrews 5:2. Jesus fulfils this by being 'made like His brothers in every way', verse 17. He goes beyond the type, for He offers Himself and not an animal, enters once for all, Hebrews 9:12, and lives forever, so that He needs no successor. The type also falls short in sin: Aaron had to offer for himself first, Leviticus 16:11, while Jesus was without sin, Hebrews 4:15.

David's psalm moves from the cry of abandonment to a vow to proclaim God's name to his brothers in the assembly, Psalm 22:22. Hebrews puts verse 22 on the lips of the risen Jesus, who stands in the congregation and sings the Father's praise with His family. The type is David as a righteous man delivered from affliction; the escalation is that the sufferer's deliverance is resurrection and that those He calls brothers are the redeemed. It falls short because David was delivered from his enemies, while Jesus was delivered out of death.

typology.type: Isaiah and the children God gave him
typology.fulfillment: In Isaiah 8:17-18 the prophet waits for the LORD and presents the children given to him as signs in Israel. Hebrews reads the voice as Christ's, who trusts the Father and presents 'the children God has given Me'. The correspondence is that of a representative standing with the ones entrusted to him. The escalation is that the children are not signs of coming judgment but of a salvation completed, and the Son is Himself the sign God gave. It falls short, as any prophet must, because Isaiah's children shared only his name and not his nature.

study.christ:
This passage does not so much lead to Christ as take the reader inside Him, and the first thing it shows is who He is, a Son with all the rank of chapter 1, now seen in the humblest place. The movement is from the throne to the 'little while' of weakness and back to the crown, and the pivot is 'we see Jesus'. In a world where the promise of Psalm 8 is not yet visible, the Christian's anchor is a person: the man who has already been crowned, and whose crowning is the pledge that the rest will follow.

The passage presents Him by pattern. Where Adam was set over creation and fell, Jesus enters creation, takes its weakness and takes its curse, and rises to the dominion Adam forfeited. Paul draws the same pattern in 1 Corinthians 15:21-28 and Romans 5:12-21, and Philippians 2:6-11 describes the same path of descent and exaltation, 'obedient to death', then 'exalted to the highest place'. The word Hebrews uses for pioneer was used of a founder of a city or a family, one who goes first and opens the way, and in Acts 5:31 the same Jesus is exalted 'as Prince and Savior'. He does not stand at the end of the road waving; He walks it first, and He leads.

It presents Him by kinship. Few verses in the New Testament are as warm as 'He is not ashamed to call them brothers'. In the Psalm 22 quotation He praises God in the midst of the assembly, and in the Isaiah quotation He stands with the children the Father gave Him. Their trust and His trust are the same trust, and His presence among them means the church's worship is never a solo.

It presents Him by victory. The enemy is not named as sin or the law but as the one who has the power of death, and the means of victory is a death. This is the strangest and the most Christian of paradoxes: the devil's strongest weapon is turned against him as the cross removes the accuser's case, Colossians 2:14-15, and fear of death, the lever by which he held people, is broken.

And it presents Him by priesthood. He is 'merciful' because He knows what we endure and 'faithful' because He completes what God asked of Him. The atonement is not set against His sympathy; they are two sides of one work. Because He suffered when He was tempted, He can sit with the tempted, not as an observer, but as one who stood in the same place, Hebrews 4:15.

The reading is kept honest by the text itself. Everything here is stated by the writer or drawn from the quoted Scriptures; nothing needs to be forced. The only things that are inferred are the voice of Christ in the two quotations, and that comes from the writer's explicit introduction, 'He says'.
study.god:
The first thing the passage says about God is a claim about His fitness to do what He does: it was fitting for the One 'for whom and through whom all things exist' to bring many sons to glory by perfecting the pioneer of their salvation through suffering. God is both the goal and the source of everything, so that His purposes cannot be thwarted or improvised. The cross is not the answer to a crisis He did not see coming. It is the chosen route of a God who is wise enough to use even humiliation to accomplish His plan.

God is the God of grace. 'By the grace of God' Jesus tastes death for everyone, verse 9. The initiative is His. The Father does not wait to be persuaded by the Son, and the Son does not drag a reluctant Father along; the passage presents the Father giving the children to the Son, verse 13, and the Son bringing them to glory. The persons are distinct in their roles, with the Father who gives, the Son who goes, yet they are one in purpose. The passage also brings in the Spirit-inspired Scripture that speaks the Son's words, verses 12 and 13, which is part of the way Hebrews weaves the three together.

God is the God who keeps His word about humanity. Psalm 8 is not an ancient daydream; the dominion promised in the psalm is held in trust, and God is committed to seeing it carried out, though 'at present we do not see'. That tension between what God has said and what we can see is a standing feature of faith, and the passage trains the reader to live inside it. God has not given up on the human race; He has sent a man to lead it home.

God is also the God who takes sin seriously. A high priest is needed because there are sins to be dealt with, verse 17, and atonement is needed because holiness is real. This is not a God who looks the other way. At the same time He is the God who provides what He demands, so that the One who makes atonement is also the One He sends. Justice and mercy are met at the same place.

God, finally, is the God who does not stand far from suffering. Pagan religion often pictured gods who are insulated from pain. Hebrews says the Son of God went through it, and that the experience has become a source of help. For worship that means the believer can approach without pretence. The right response to this God is not to put on a brave face but to bring the weakness and the temptation to the One who is 'able to help', and to trust that the God who is above all things is also near to the weak.

crossReferences.note: The source text. The psalm's wonder at human significance is quoted in the Greek version, with angels where the Hebrew has Elohim. Hebrews reads the psalm as a promise that sin delayed, and sees it kept in the one true man, so that the lovely lines about dominion become a statement about Jesus and those who are in Him.

The creation mandate behind the psalm. Humanity is made in God's image and told to rule over the living creatures. The note of 'not yet' in Hebrews 2:8 makes sense only against this: the first commission was given in Genesis, lost in Genesis 3, and now renewed through Jesus.

Paul quotes the same line from Psalm 8, 'God has put everything under His feet', and spells out the timetable. Christ reigns until every enemy is put down, the last enemy being death. It fills in the 'not yet' of Hebrews 2:8 by describing the stages by which all things come to be under Him.

A parallel path of descent and exaltation. He did not grasp at equality with God but emptied Himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death, and so God exalted Him. Hebrews gives the same story in the language of Psalm 8: made lower for a little while, now crowned with glory and honour.

The verse Hebrews puts on the lips of Jesus. The psalm moves from the sufferer's cry to a promise to tell God's name to his brothers, and ends by saying God did not hide His face from the afflicted. Hebrews hears the risen Christ leading the congregation's praise, with the redeemed as His brothers.

The prophet says he will wait for the LORD and trust Him, and presents the children given to him as signs. Hebrews uses the two halves to show Christ's trust in the Father and His presentation of the family the Father gave Him, so that faith and fellowship are placed together in one scene.

The Day of Atonement, where the high priest takes the goat's blood behind the veil and makes atonement for the sanctuary and the people. It is the background to 'make atonement for the sins of the people' in verse 17, and it shows why a priest needed to be both a man and acceptable to God.

The next stage of the priestly argument, and it repeats the sympathy of 2:17-18 in almost the same terms. Jesus is a high priest who can sympathize with weakness, tempted in every way yet without sin, and so we may approach the throne of grace with confidence to find mercy and help.

Another look at the perfecting of verse 10. Here it takes the form of prayers with loud cries and tears, a Son who 'learned obedience from what He suffered', and the result that He became the source of eternal salvation. It shows what the word 'suffering' meant in practice: not pain alone, but the long obedience of a man in prayer.

The Son of God was revealed 'to destroy the works of the devil'. It matches the purpose clause of Hebrews 2:14 from a different angle. John gives the aim, Hebrews gives the means: He shared our flesh and blood so that through death He might break the one who held the power of death.

The same word for pioneer returns in the letter's great call to endurance. Jesus is the 'author and perfecter of our faith', who endured the cross for the joy set before Him and sat down at God's right hand. The pioneer of 2:10 is the runner who has finished the course and now stands at the finish.

God sent His own Son 'in the likeness of sinful man' to deal with sin. It lines up with Hebrews 2:14 and 2:17, where the Son takes our flesh to condemn sin and to make atonement. Both writers insist on a real incarnation without any trace of sin in the Son.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a king and his kingdom in miniature: humanity crowned with glory and honour in a garden, charged to rule the world and to keep it, Genesis 1:26-28. Hebrews 2 takes up that opening commission in the light of everything that has happened since, and it names the problem plainly: 'we do not see everything subject to him'. Sin did not cancel the calling, but it left humanity ruling badly and dying. The long middle of the Bible, from the promise of Genesis 3:15 to the sacrifices of Leviticus, is God working out how the crown can be restored without the sin being ignored.

This passage answers that question with a person. The Son enters the story as one of the family, shares its flesh and blood, and becomes both the champion who wins and the priest who atones. The Bible's two threads, kingship and priesthood, which have run side by side through Israel's history, are woven into one person. He is the true man who rules, and the true priest who covers, and the second cannot be done without the first being dead and alive again.

It also gives the middle of the story its shape. The 'little while' of verse 9 is the time of the church, the time between the crowning and the final subjecting of all things. Believers live in it as brothers among brothers, singing in the assembly, tested as He was tested and helped by the One who knows what testing is. The family language reaches back to Israel's sons and forward to the church, where those who belong to Christ are called the descendants of Abraham, Galatians 3:29.

The end of the story is the full seeing of what we now hold by faith. Death, 'the last enemy', is destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:26, and the one who holds its power is cast out. Creation, which was 'subjected to futility', is set free, Romans 8:20-21, and the saints reign, Revelation 22:5. The dominion of Psalm 8, lost in a garden, is restored in a city where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3-4, and the human race, led home by its pioneer, finally stands crowned beside Him.

quiz.q: Why did the exalted Son become lower than the angels for a while?

options.text: To share our humanity, taste death for everyone, and become our merciful high priest.
options.note: Verses 9 to 17 give exactly these reasons.

options.text: Because He was demoted for a failure.
options.note: He was not demoted; He willingly took our nature to save us.

options.text: To become permanently inferior to the angels.
options.note: It was for a little while, and He is now crowned with glory above the angels.

options.text: Only to set a good moral example.
options.note: He does set an example, but the deeper purpose was atonement and deliverance.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Jesus was 'made perfect' through suffering?

options.text: He was fully qualified and completed for His saving work as our high priest.
options.note: Perfecting here is vocational completeness, not the removal of sin.
The letter insists Jesus was without sin throughout.

options.text: He became a better teacher through practice.
options.note: It concerns His fitness to save, not merely His teaching skill.

options.text: He earned His divinity by effort.
options.note: He was already the divine Son; the perfecting fitted Him as Saviour and priest.

quiz.q: What did Jesus accomplish by sharing our flesh and blood and dying?

options.text: He destroyed the devil's power of death and freed those enslaved by fear of death.
He proved that death always wins.
options.note: He defeated death, breaking its power.
He helps the descendants of Abraham, not angels.

options.text: He removed all physical suffering immediately.
options.note: He frees from the slavery of fear, though bodily suffering remains for now.

quiz.q: Why is Jesus able to help those who are tempted?

options.text: Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted.
options.note: Verse 18 grounds His help in His own tested experience.

options.text: Because He never faced any temptation.
options.note: He was tempted; that is precisely why He can help.

options.text: Because He keeps His distance from our struggles.
options.note: He drew near, sharing our nature and testing.

options.text: Because temptation is not really serious.
options.note: Temptation is serious; He helps because He knows it firsthand.

questions: We do not yet see everything subject to us, but we see Jesus crowned. How does fixing your eyes on Him help when the world looks out of control?
Jesus tasted death for everyone. What does it mean to you that the Son of God went through death ahead of you as your pioneer?
Jesus is not ashamed to call you His brother or sister. How does that change the way you come to Him with your weakness and sin?
He came to free those enslaved by the fear of death. Where does fear of death, or of loss, still hold power over you?
Our high priest was tempted and is able to help. What temptation could you bring to Him honestly this week, expecting help?

translationNotes.note: The phrase 'a little lower than the angels' can also be rendered 'for a little while lower', a nuance that fits the temporary humbling of the Son before His exaltation.
'Author' renders archēgos, which can also be translated pioneer or founder; it pictures a trailblazer who goes first and leads others along the way.
'Make atonement' translates a verb that can also be rendered 'make propitiation'; it carries the sense of turning away wrath by a sufficient sacrifice.
